the unfolding of a ubiquitin +13 protein ion occurs in three steps, and the unfolding rate at 300 K is 2 ms.
the unfolding of ubiquitin +13 in the gas phase proceeds via a series of intermediate states, and that the rate of unfolding is on a time scale that is accessible to molecular dynamics simulations.

the conformational evolution of an ubiquitin + 13 ion system in electrospray experiments is described by a three-state model and that the rate constant for the unfolding of this system is calculated to be 2.2 x 10(5) s(-1).

the conformational evolution of an ubiquitin + 13 ion system in mass spectrometry and the development of a new approach to the unfolding of proteins.
a theoretical description of the conformational evolution of a protein in electrospray experiments.
the development of a molecular dynamics based approach for the study of unfolding processes of protein ions in electrosprays and other mass spectrometric environments.

the conformational evolution of a folded protein in mass spectrometry is a complex process that involves several intermediate states and a near linear structure as the final state.
ubiquitin ions are in the near linear state in the electrospray mass spectrum.
the ubiquitin +13 unfolding process in mass spectrometry is a slow one, and that the final near linear structure is formed at the experimental temperatures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the unfolding process of a protein in mass spectrometry can be described as an energy barrier crossing problem, which can be treated by molecular dynamics simulations and the RRK model.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the unfolding process of ubiquitin +13 in electrospray experiments is not a fast process and occurs at a time scale of 2 ms.
unfolding of a protein in a mass spectrometer is not a single-step process but a multi-step process.

the conformational evolution of the ubiquitin +13 system can be described in terms of a series of energy barriers and that the unfolding process can be understood in terms of a Rice-Ramspeger-Kassel (or RRK) type of approach.
